palette.role: Evergreen cover, autumn nectar and winter berries, only where attachment, inspection and spread can be controlled.

attachment.supportNeeds: Clings to the timber unaided. Bound its sectors and inspect joints: stems that enter gaps thicken and can force members apart.

wood.basis: Inferred; no source puts it in pruning terms. The flowers are carried in a terminal cluster of umbels on the bushy adult shoots and never on the climbing shoots (Bean, Trees and Shrubs Online), from September to November (RHS), so they end that year's adult growth. What governs flowering is the growth phase, not the age of the wood: adult growth appears after about ten years, and regular pruning keeps ivy juvenile and non-flowering (RHS ivy guide).

monthsUK.basis: RHS (ivy on buildings and fences): the mature stage "bears clusters of yellow-green flowers in rounded heads from September to November". Stated in months. Bean (Trees and Shrubs Online) says October; the RHS record says autumn and the RHS ivy guide late autumn.

flowering.display: Nectar-rich greenish flowers on adult shoots, then black berries in winter.

site.aspect: Shade to sun; exposed or sheltered.
site.soil: Broadly tolerant; fertile and well-drained preferred.

calendar.note: RHS ivy guide: trim back excess growth in mid-spring; an overgrown plant can be hard pruned in early spring. RHS record: pruning group 11, at any time. Check for nesting birds first: the nesting season generally runs from March to August (RHS).

management.notes: Hold it to explicit boundaries; cut back and remove encroachment periodically; keep every timber junction exposed for inspection.

hazards: Stems can enter gaps in wooden structures, thicken and push sections apart (RHS, ivy on buildings).

sources.label: RHS: ivy on buildings and fences
RHS: pruning established climbers (pruning groups 11 to 13)
